Summon: Bahamut: Late-game bomb, but read the split: 51.4% from the opening hand versus 59.9% drawn. Nine mana is a dead card early even though chapters I and II are unconditional permanent removal. First-pickable at ALSA 1.5, and it wins the game the turn it resolves — just don't build around casting it on curve.
Ultima, Origin of Oblivion: Trap-adjacent rare. A colorless 5-mana 4/4 flier taken at pick 2.6 that only returns 53.0% (IWD +1.0) — the land-blighting is win-more and the body dies to everything while the ground is already clogged. Playable in any deck, but never over real removal or a cheap evasive threat.
Adelbert Steiner: Solid two-drop, but a WR-specific one. The 58.1% next to a mere +1.5 IWD is the classic 'good decks run this' shape — he's a 2/1 that dies to everything unless equipment is already stacked. Take him high only once you're in WR Job Select; elsewhere he's filler.
Aerith Gainsborough: Solid playable, not the bomb her ALSA 2.4 implies. A three-mana 2/2 lifelink that only snowballs if you already have lifegain, and the death trigger needs other legends — 55.2% with IWD +1.0 says she is a fine WB/WG body, not a first-pick rare.
Aerith Rescue Mission: Filler, and only a third of decks played it. Four mana for three 1/1s adds bodies to a board that is already gummed up, and the tap mode is a one-shot Falter. The +1.7 gd/oh split says it is a late-game mana sink, not a card you want early. Last playable in WR/WG go-wide.
Ambrosia Whiteheart: Solid playable, not a premium pick. Flash evasion at two matters in a format that stalls on the ground, but the 56.4% with IWD only +0.3 is the classic "good decks run this" shape — it rides your deck rather than winning games. Best in WU/WR where the ETB rebuys an equipment or Job Select trigger.
Ashe, Princess of Dalmasca: Role-player, not the early pick her 4.5 ALSA implies. A 3/2 for three dies to everything in a removal-dense format and the attack trigger whiffs unless you're in artifact-heavy WU/WR. 54.7% with IWD -1.5 is the 'good decks run it' shape.
Auron's Inspiration: Trap-ish filler. A three-mana attack pump plus a five-mana flashback is exactly the card a removal-dense, gummed-up format punishes — 52.5% with IWD −3.4 says drawing it actively hurts. Only a WR Job Select deck with a real go-wide board should sideboard it in.
Battle Menu: High-floor playable, near-auto-include at 89% play. The Magic mode only answers power 4+, so it is conditional removal, but a format of 3/3s and 4-toughness bodies means the 2/2 or the +0/+4 combat blowout is usually the live mode. IWD +1.9 says convenient, not game-breaking.
Cloud, Midgar Mercenary: Premium early pick for WR/WU equipment — a two-drop that tutors the Job Select piece you're missing and then doubles its triggers. OH 60.2% beating GD 57.5% says cast it turn two and build around it; the 2/1 body dies to everything, so the tutor is the floor.
Cloudbound Moogle: Filler. Five mana for a 2/3 flier is a bad rate even in a format that pays for evasion, and 52.1% with IWD -2.1 and a 21% play rate says most W drafters correctly leave it out. The Plains-cycling is the real reason it's in your 40 at all.
Coeurl: Filler. A 2/2 that taps a blocker for {1}{W} sounds fine, but in a clogged removal-heavy format a repeatable tapper that costs two mana per activation is too slow, and 53.9% with IWD -1.5 confirms it. Playable filler in WR aggro, last cards of the deck elsewhere.
Crystal Fragments: Trap uncommon. A one-mana +1/+1 stick with a seven-mana flip you rarely reach, and 52.4% with IWD -1.7 says drawing it actively hurts. Only playable as the 23rd card in a WR equipment deck that needs cheap artifact count.
The Crystal's Chosen: Solid top-end payoff for go-wide white, not a bomb. Seven mana for four bodies plus a team-wide counter is exactly the card that breaks a WG/WR board stall, and 57.0% with a +3.9 gap between opening-hand and drawn WR says it's a late-game card you want to draw, not keep. One copy only.
Delivery Moogle: High pick in any equipment deck. A four-mana flier is already above rate in a format where evasion breaks the ground stall, and the tutor grabs Job Select gear from library or yard, so it's never a blank. 60.0%/+2.9 is real; WR and WU want it early.
Dion, Bahamut's Dominant: First-pick bomb, no discussion. 64.5% GIH with IWD +10.8 and ALSA 1.4 — a four-mana 3/3 that brings a 2/2 body, grants your team attacking flight in a format where evasion breaks the stall, and flips into a Saga that destroys a permanent. Take it over anything.
Dragoon's Lance: Premium uncommon and a top-3 white card at 61.6% / IWD +6.3 with a 2.7 ALSA — take it over most removal. Job Select means it eats a removal spell and still leaves a flying attacker, and evasion is exactly what breaks this format's ground stall. WR and WU both want it.
Dwarven Castle Guard: Filler for aggressive white decks only. A 2/1 is on the wrong side of the format's 3/3-and-4-toughness ground stall, and the death token is a chump, not value; 54.1% with IWD -1.5 and a 6.3 ALSA confirms it's a late-pack body. Playable in WR curve decks, cuttable everywhere else.
Fate of the Sun-Cryst: Playable catch-all removal, but your fifth or sixth piece, not your first. Five mana at full price is unaffordable; you only get the discount punishing an attacker, so it never answers the blocker gumming up the ground. 54.1% sits far below Sephiroth's Intervention.
From Father to Son: Near-unplayable rare; 1.1% play rate means drafters correctly cut it. A two-mana tutor that finds one Vehicle is card disadvantage unless you already have a bomb Vehicle, and the flashback costs seven. Read is provisional with no WR data, but treat it as a blank.
G'raha Tia: Filler. Five mana for a 3/5 reach body with no ETB is exactly the trap shape the doctrine flags — the draw trigger needs your own stuff dying, which is not a plan you build around. IWD -0.3 confirms it is a body you cut when better fives show up.
Gaelicat: Solid playable, not a slam: a three-mana vigilant flier that turns into a 3/3 flier once you have two artifacts, which is easy in WU/WR. The 56.7% with IWD -0.3 is the classic 'good decks run this' shape — it's a fine deck-filler that evades the ground stall, not a card that wins games alone.
Machinist's Arsenal: Premium — take it over most removal. Job Select means it's a two-for-one that also eats a kill spell, and +2/+2 per artifact scales fast in WU/WR builds. 58.9% at ALSA 2.1 with an 89% play rate: it performs at the price people pay.
Magitek Armor: Solid playable, effectively a 4/4 plus a 1/1 body for four. The token crews it immediately so it isn't a real vehicle liability, and the four-toughness attacker sits above the format's cheap removal. 57.1% at ALSA 4.6 with 78% play rate — a fine mid-pack pickup for WR or WU.
Magitek Infantry: Textbook high-GIH / negative-IWD card: 58.1% looks premium but IWD -0.8 means good WU/WR artifact decks run it, it does not win games. The tutor ability is a mana sink, not card advantage. Playable filler in an artifact deck, never a reason to be in white.
Minwu, White Mage: Skip it. A 3/3 vigilance lifelink for five is fine on rate but 51.6% GIH with IWD −1.5 at ALSA 3.3 is the classic over-drafted rare — the Cleric counter clause is nearly blank in FIN, and five mana for a body that trades with commons loses the midrange race. Take the removal.
Moogles' Valor: Strong but conditional — it's a combat blowout plus a go-wide burst, and the 60.6 drawn vs 56.5 opening-hand split says it needs a board first. Five mana at instant speed wrecks a stalled ground, which is exactly FIN's default. Best in WG/WR; near-dead in a low-creature build.
Paladin's Arms: Playable WR/WU equipment glue, not a priority. 55.8% GIH with IWD −0.9 is the classic "good decks run this" shape — Job Select gives you a body plus ward {1} that eats a removal spell, but equip {4} is punishing and it does nothing in a deck without cheap creatures.
Phoenix Down: Trap-ish filler at 52.2% with negative IWD despite the one-mana price. Two-mana activation on a body of MV4 or less is fine value in BG/WB grind, but it does nothing to the board the turn you cast it and half the mode is a dead sideboard clause. Playable only with real reanimation targets.
Restoration Magic: Better than its +1.4 IWD looks — take it as a real playable in any white deck. LoL called it a top-two card in the format, and the split (58.3% drawn vs 55.3% opening hand) says the same thing: it's a reactive card you hold, blanking removal or Curaga-ing a whole board through a sweeper or a combat blowout.
Sidequest: Catch a Fish: Near-filler. Three mana that does nothing to the board, needs a creature/artifact-dense curve to trigger reliably, and the pump side costs six. 50.5% with IWD -3.0 and a 20% play rate is the format telling you it's a 23rd card.
Slash of Light: Solid white common removal that scales with your board — cheap, instant-speed, and it clears four-toughness once you have three bodies plus an Equipment. The 56.7% with IWD only +0.1 tells you it's board-dependent, not a standalone answer: great in WR/WG go-wide, weak in a stalled draw.
Snow Villiers: Near-sideboard. A three-mana */3 whose power is your board count is worst precisely when you are behind, and a removal-dense format keeps your board small. IWD -3.0 and 47% play rate are damning; only WG go-wide should even consider it.
Stiltzkin, Moogle Merchant: Trap rare, and the doctrine names it as one (52.8%, IWD -1.7). Donating a permanent to draw one card at two mana a pop is a slow, board-losing engine in a removal-dense midrange format. The 52% play rate says half the drafters who open it already know. Pass for any common removal spell.
Summon: Choco/Mog: Marginal playable. A 3/3 for three that self-destructs after four turns, with a pump that only matters if you're already wide — and this format's boards gum up rather than race. 53.4% with IWD -1.9 confirms it: fine 22nd card in WG/WR go-wide, never a pick you're happy about.
Summon: Knights of Round: Bomb. Eight mana is real, but four chapters of three 2/2s each plus an indestructible-anthem finish ends any board stall outright, and the 3/3 indestructible body survives everything. 59.2%, IWD +5.9, ALSA 1.6 — first-pickable if you can support {W}{W} and get to eight.
Summon: Primal Garuda: Solid playable, not a premium pick. A 3/3 flier for four is exactly what breaks this format's ground stall, but chapter I only hits tapped creatures, so treat it as a body first. IWD +1.7 against 56.7% GIH marks it as a good deck's card, mid-pack in WU or WG.
Ultima: Situational rare, not the sweeper its name suggests. Five mana one-sided-never wrath that also blanks your own board; 55.2% and IWD +3.1 mean it's fine, but it only shines from behind against go-wide WR/WG. Build a controlling UB/WB deck around surviving to cast it, or leave it in the board.
Venat, Heart of Hydaelyn: Fine rare, not a bomb. The 3/3 for three is a real body with four-toughness-adjacent staying power once the flip side starts handing out counters and indestructible, but the draw trigger only pays in a legend-dense WB/WG deck. 58.2%/+3.6 says good, ALSA 2.0 says overdrafted.
Weapons Vendor: Late filler for equipment decks only. A four-mana 2/2 that replaces itself is fine on rate, but IWD −1.6 and a 62.7% play rate mark it as a body you play when WR/WU is already assembled. Never move in on it; wheel it.
White Auracite: Premium common removal in disguise: 59.4% / +3.5 at a 3.2 ALSA, catch-all exile on any nonland permanent, and it taps for white afterward. The double-white and the fact that it can be blown up are real, but this answers four-toughness creatures white otherwise can't. Take it early in any W deck.
White Mage's Staff: Strong white common, take it around pick 3-5. Job Select means it's two cards of pressure that also demands a removal spell — and remember the format rule: killing the equipped 1/1 is usually right, so expect the same from opponents. The 59.4% opening-hand number marks it as a curve card for WR/WU aggro.
The Wind Crystal: Trap — one of the set's headline early-pick rares that doesn't perform (50.9%, IWD -1.6, taken at 4.1). Four mana that doesn't touch the board is unaffordable when the ground clogs, and the flying alley costs six more. Being a rare Crystal is not a reason.
You're Not Alone: Combat trick, not a priority. One mana for +4/+4 with three creatures out genuinely blows out the format's 3/3 ground mirrors, but IWD −1.1 and 45.5% play rate mark it as a deck-specific card. Play one in WR or WG aggro, none anywhere else.
Zack Fair: Solid early playable, better than it looks. A one-mana body that later blanks a removal spell on your best creature and relocates its counters and Equipment — LoL's "annoyingly good" read is correct. OH 58.9% > GD 56.8% marks it as a curve card, and it shines in WR/WB equipment builds.
Astrologian's Planisphere: Premium uncommon-quality rare: 57.7% with IWD +4.5 and a 91.7% play rate at ALSA 2.1. Job Select means it eats a removal spell for you, and the counters snowball fast in UR or WU spells decks that already cast noncreature spells and dig. Take it early and equip it back onto a real body later.
Cargo Ship: Role-player for WU artifacts. A two-mana 2/3 flier is exactly the evasion that breaks the ground stall, and crew 1 is trivially met, but three toughness dies to everything and the artifact-mana clause is nearly blank. 54.5%/+1.8 is honest mid-table; take it after real playables.
Combat Tutorial: Premium common — take it over most creatures. Three mana draw-two with a counter attached is pure card advantage in a grindy midrange format, and LoL calls it the #1 blue common in retrospect. 58.9% with IWD +4.6 confirms; blue's best non-removal common in UR or UB.
Dragoon's Wyvern: Premium common — take it over most uncommons. Three mana for a flier plus a Hero token is two bodies and real evasion in a format that stalls on the ground, and 90% play rate at ALSA 4.0 means it wheels far later than it should. LoL landed on top-3 common overall and the best blue common for UR.
Dreams of Laguna: Excellent common glue for any blue deck. Two-mana cantrip with surveil that comes back for four is two cards from one slot, and 57.9% / +3.1 at ALSA 5.2 means it consistently wheels. Great in UR tiered-spell decks and UB grind; not a first pick, but it makes every blue deck's 23.
Edgar, King of Figaro: Trap unless you're genuinely artifact-heavy. Six mana for a 4/5 whose ETB frequently draws one or zero is exactly the expensive-no-real-ETB shape this removal-dense format punishes — 49.6% opening-hand and a 54% play rate confirm it. Only a WU/UR artifact deck should maindeck it.
Eject: Premium blue interaction — the doctrine benchmark at 59.2% GIH, IWD +5.0. Uncounterable bounce plus a card answers anything, including the four-toughness bodies and equipped Job Select tokens that gum the ground up. OH 55.9 vs GD 61.2 says hold it; it is a mid-game tempo card, not a curve play.
Ether: Trap outside a dedicated spells build — 49.7% GIH and a 13% play rate say most drafters correctly cut it. LoL's eight-card story is the ceiling, not the median; a four-mana artifact that does nothing on arrival is exactly what this removal-dense format punishes. Sideboard unless UR is deep in tiered spells.
Gogo, Master of Mimicry: Overdrafted at 3.3 ALSA for what it does. The 2/4 body is genuinely good here — four toughness survives the format's cheap removal — but the {X}{X} copy ability is a mana sink that needs a build-around, and 51.7% with -0.2 IWD and a 48.7% opening-hand rate proves it isn't winning games. Play it as a blocker, never take it over removal.
Ice Flan: Fine top-end common, late pick. Six mana for a 5/4 plus a stun counter is real tempo, and islandcycling {2} means it's never a dead card in a flooded or screwed draw. The +0.5 IWD and 6.7 ALSA say curve-filler, not priority.
Ice Magic: Premium blue common — take it in the first few picks. The Blizzard tier gives you a two-mana tempo answer to anything at any point on the curve, and Blizzaga permanently deals with a bomb. LoL is right; 58.2% / +3.5 puts it alongside the best black commons.
Il Mheg Pixie: Premium two-drop, take it over most commons. Evasion is what breaks FIN's ground stall, and a 2/1 flier that surveils each attack fixes draws while it clocks. 58.0% with +3.4 IWD and 92% play across UR/WU/UB — it fits everywhere blue does.
Jill, Shiva's Dominant: Bomb, first pick out of any pack. 62.6% GIH with IWD +9.4 is top-of-set territory: a three-mana tempo bounce on a body that later flips into a Saga that unblocks your team and taps their lands. Blue is the best colour and this is one of the reasons.
Louisoix's Sacrifice: Sideboard. Countering only noncreature spells and abilities in a creature-and-removal midrange format means it's dead too often, and the sacrifice-a-legend clause is a tax you'll almost always pay in mana. 48.2% with a 43.6% opening-hand WR and 9% play rate — leave it in the board.
The Lunar Whale: Near-bomb rare. A 3/5 flier crewed by any one creature is both the evasion that breaks stalls and a four-toughness wall, and the top-of-library access turns a stalled board into card advantage. 59.3%, IWD +5.8, ALSA 2.0 — first pick in blue, and the crew-1 means it needs no aggro shell.
Magic Damper: Role-player, not maindeck filler by default. A one-mana untap-plus-hexproof blanks a removal spell and steals a combat in a format packing 4-6 pieces of interaction. The 32% play rate and ALSA 7.4 say it's a late-pick you add when your deck already has creatures worth protecting.
Matoya, Archon Elder: Leave it unless you're deep in surveil. The 1/4 body sits well against the format's 3-power ground, but 38.9% play rate and 51.7% GIH show blue drafters correctly cut it — FIN doesn't have enough scry/surveil density to make a three-mana do-nothing pay off. Sideboard card in UB.
Memories Returning: Premium card advantage. Three cards for four mana with a late flashback, and +6.0 IWD means it genuinely wins games rather than just riding good decks. It doesn't touch the board, so pair it with your 4-6 removal spells; UR and UB grinds want it as an early pick.
The Prima Vista: Marginal top-end, a UR-only consideration. Five mana for a 5/3 flier that needs crew 2 or a big tiered spell to attack, and 52.0% GIH with 25% play rate says it mostly sat in sideboards. Take real evasion or removal instead.
Qiqirn Merchant: Marginal playable at 52.8% and a 34.7% play rate. The 1/4 body is the right size to brick the ground, but looting for {1} is slow and the sac ability needs a Town count you shouldn't be drafting toward. Late-pick blocker for UB/UG grind; the doctrine warns against chasing Towns.
Quistis Trepe: Solid value uncommon for UB/UR, weak on curve. The gap between 58.8% drawn and 51.1% in opening hands is the whole story: a 2/2 for three is nothing early, but late it rebuys your best removal spell off any graveyard with any mana. Prioritize it only once your deck is interaction-dense.
Relm's Sketching: Solid playable that scales with your board — copy your best creature or an opposing bomb. Note gd 57.9% vs oh 51.4%: this is a card you want to draw late, not keep in an opener. Best in UG and WU where the targets are big.
Retrieve the Esper: Strong blue common: a four-mana 3/3 that comes back from the graveyard as a 5/5 is two bodies with four toughness, exactly what breaks ground stalls. The OH 53.0 vs GD 57.2 split confirms Numot's read — it's a late-game card, so don't keep it as your early play.
Rook Turret: Filler flier. Four mana for a 3/3 in the air should be fine, but 51.8% and a 33% play rate say the looting rarely turns on outside a real artifact count. Playable in WU artifacts as a late body, otherwise leave it.
Sage's Nouliths: Filler at best — the weakest Job Select in the set (52.8%, ALSA 6.9, 39% play rate). +1/+0 and a Vigilance-ish untap doesn't threaten anything in a format where four toughness is the bar, and equip {3} means you're never moving it. Play it only as a 23rd card in an equipment-saturated WR deck.
Sahagin: Core UR common — take it highly if you're in tiered spells. The counter plus unblockable turns a defensive 1/3 into a real clock the same turn your MV4+ spell resolves, and it blocks the format's ground creatures until then. 58.1%/+3.0 at 82% play rate is genuinely strong for a common.
Scorpion Sentinel: Underdrafted common that overperforms — 1/4 for two blanks the format's ground creatures and later becomes a 4/4. LoL's read holds: this is blue's defensive backbone. 56.0% with +1.6 at ALSA 5.9 means you get it late; take it in any UX deck that wants to reach the mid-game.
Sidequest: Card Collection: Strong blue uncommon and a real pick. Four mana for net-plus-one card that fuels the graveyard, then flips into a flying vehicle so it isn't stranded late. 59.1% with IWD +4.6 and a big drawn-over-opening gap: it's a mid-game engine, not a keep-worthy opener.
Sleep Magic: Premium blue removal at one mana. It answers the four-toughness bodies cheap burn can't, and 58.8% / +4.3 at 89.2% play rate puts it right on the Ice Magic / Swallowed by Leviathan tier while costing a single pip. The damage clause is a real drawback, but take it over any non-removal uncommon.
Stolen Uniform: Sideboard at best. Borrowing an opponent's Equipment for one turn does almost nothing when the format's Job Select gear is attached to a 1/1 they're happy to lose. Null WR with a 0.7% play rate and ALSA 8.7 — the read is provisional, but nobody plays it for a reason.
Stuck in Summoner's Sanctum: Fine blue common, a clear step below Ice Magic. Flash pacifism that also shuts off activated abilities and equipment, but the creature stays on defense as a blocker-in-name only. OH 51.4 vs GD 57.5 — dead in your opener, good on turn six.
Summon: Leviathan: Bomb-adjacent rare at 58.9% / +5.7, first-pickable at ALSA 2.0. Chapter I is a one-sided Evacuation that resets the clogged ground and leaves you a 6/6 with ward 2 — exactly the kind of stall-breaker blue wants. Six mana is real, so back it with cheap interaction.
Summon: Shiva: Strong blue uncommon — take it highly. Two turns of stun-tapping is pseudo-removal in a stall format, the 4/5 sits above every cheap removal spell while it's on board, and chapter III refuels. Five mana keeps it out of opening hands (53.1% OH vs 58.5% drawn), but +3.0 IWD says it earns its slot.
Swallowed by Leviathan: Premium blue interaction and a top-tier uncommon (59.3%, IWD +4.7). LoL and Numot agree it only gets better as graveyards fill — surveil 2 first means it's a hard counter by mid-game. Take it over almost any creature; UR and WU want it most.
Syncopate: Take it and play it. The experts converged hard here: a scaling counter that exiles is the best cheap blue interaction in a format where the graveyard matters, and 57.5% / +3.5 backs the retro read that it kept climbing. Core UR and UB card.
Thief's Knife: Marginal Job Select. The 2/2 hero that draws on connect looks fine, but equip {4} means it never moves, and per doctrine your opponent just kills the 1/1 and eats the whole card. 52.5% with +0.3 IWD — playable filler in WU/WR equipment, not a payoff.
Travel the Overworld: Late-game value card, not an early pick. GD 58.7% against OH 53.1% is the tell: it's dead in your opener and great on turn seven-plus. Only worth a slot in UG/UB grind decks that already collected three or four Towns organically — never take a Town early to enable it.
Ultros, Obnoxious Octopus: Strong UR uncommon, near-premium. Two mana that converts every big tiered spell into a Frost Titan trigger — tapping and stunning a blocker is removal-adjacent in a stalled format. 58.2%/+3.7 at ALSA 3.7; the eight-mana mode is win-more, ignore it when evaluating.
Valkyrie Aerial Unit: Sideboard-to-filler outside a real artifact count. Seven mana with affinity is a trap number unless you have four-plus artifacts, and the 5/4 flier dies to everything red or black. 52.6% GIH with OH 49.9% says it's a late-game card in a specific WU/UR artifact deck, not a general playable.
The Water Crystal: Trap rare — 46.7% GIH and a 10.6% play rate mean drafters correctly cut it. The cost reduction wants a dedicated blue deck and the mill plan doesn't kill anyone in a midrange format. Same family as the other Crystals the doctrine flags: rarity is not a reason to take it.
Y'shtola Rhul: Strong but conditional mythic. Six mana for a 3/5 that does nothing on its own — the value comes from a board of ETB creatures and doubled end steps, so it's a UB/UG value payoff, not a slam. 55.6% with IWD +4.5 says it wins the games it stabilizes; ALSA 2.5 says the field overvalues it.
Ahriman: Playable filler, not a priority. Flying deathtouch on a three-mana body trades up and pokes through a clogged board, but 2/2 dies to every cheap removal spell and the sac-draw costs too much to use twice. 54.6%/+0.7 is a mid-common; BG sac decks value it slightly higher.
Al Bhed Salvagers: Solid uncommon body for BG and WB. A 2/3 for three that drains every time anything of yours dies converts the format's clogged-ground trades into reach, and 56.0% with GD 57.3 says it compounds the longer the game runs. Mid-pack pick, better with tokens.
Ardyn, the Usurper: Outright bomb: 64.5% GIH and IWD +12.0 are among the highest numbers in the set, and it's a 4/4 that makes a hasty menace-lifelink 5/5 every combat off any graveyard. Eight mana is the only obstacle, and BG/BR games run that long. First pick, build the mana.
Black Mage's Rod: Good black common, best in spell-heavy UB/BR builds. Same Job Select math as the other equipment — a two-mana 2/1 that also eats a removal spell — with the ping upside turning every burn spell and cantrip into reach. LoL's read holds; +1.6 IWD is real but this is a mid-pack pick, not an early one.
Cecil, Dark Knight: First-pickable rare. A one-mana 2/3 deathtouch blanks the format's default 3/3 ground stall on turn one and stays relevant to turn ten, then flips into a lifelink finisher on its own. 58.3% with IWD +4.9 at a 2.3 ALSA is real; take it.
Circle of Power: Excellent black uncommon — a four-mana Divination stapled to a token that pings, and the Wizard buff occasionally steals a race. 57.5% with ALSA 4.2 says it's raw card advantage that any black deck wants; the Wizard subtheme is upside, not a requirement.
Cornered by Black Mages: Premium common, take it early. Three-mana edict that also leaves a Wizard pinger, and in a removal-dense format you strip their one real threat often enough. LoL is right that it scales with your other removal — the more you have, the fewer bodies they keep. 58.3%, +4.1.
Dark Confidant: Strong but curve-dependent, on a bonus-sheet sample of a few thousand games so treat 59.4% as noisy. OH 63.9% vs GD 56.2% confirms it wants to land on turn two before your top-end lands. Fine in aggressive WB/BR builds with cheap spells; don't run it alongside six-drops.
Dark Knight's Greatsword: Solid playable, best in WR/WB aggro. Job Select gives you a body plus a threat that must be answered twice, and equipping for life instead of mana is genuinely free on a curve turn. But +3/+0 with no evasion stalls out on the format's clogged ground — 55.8%/+1.8 is good, not premium.
The Darkness Crystal: Trap-adjacent rare, same family as the other Crystals. Four mana that does nothing on arrival is brutal in a removal-dense clogged format; the exile-replacement only matters once you already have the board. 53.6% at ALSA 3.6 means people take it early and pay for it — a late-pick at best.
Demon Wall: Fine two-drop role-player for BG or WB. A 3/3 defender for two brick-walls the format's ground creatures early, and menace plus the counter mode gives it late-game attack reach. 54.8% with IWD +1.2 is honest: it holds serve, it doesn't take over.
Evil Reawakened: Best-in-class BG payoff at uncommon. Five mana to rebuy your best creature with two counters usually rebuilds a board and blanks their removal spell; 57.0% / +3.9 with the drawn WR five points above opening-hand confirms it's a mid-game card you cast, not one you mulligan for. Prioritize once you have targets.
Fang, Fearless l'Cie: Skip it outside a built graveyard deck. A 2/3 that does nothing on its own, and 51.2% with a negative IWD and 56% play rate is a rare uncommon that actively costs you games. You need real flashback and recursion density before the draw trigger is more than a maybe.
Fight On!: Grindy BG filler. Double raise dead at instant speed is real card advantage in a removal-dense format, but it costs you a turn and does nothing to the board — OH 50.3 vs GD 57.0, a card you want as your 22nd, never your 15th.
The Final Days: Solid playable that's better in BG than the 56.6% suggests. Four mana for two tapped 2/2s is unexciting on rate, but the flashback lets you cash a stocked graveyard for a genuine army, and +1.6 IWD understates a card whose second cast wins the game. Fine in WB too as raw bodies.
Gaius van Baelsar: Role-player, not a bomb signpost. The edict modes are symmetric, so you need a spare Hero token or a board they can't afford to trim, and a 3/2 for four is instantly outclassed on this ground. 54.8% and +1.0 make it a fine WB/BG 22nd card that occasionally answers a bomb they hid behind tokens.
Hecteyes: Fine early-game common, not a priority. The 1/1 body is irrelevant in a four-toughness format — you're paying two mana for a discard that's only a real card when cast on turn two. 56.0% with IWD +1.2 makes it a solid 20th-23rd card in BG or UB.
Jecht, Reluctant Guardian: Real rare. A 4/3 menace connects in this format more often than you'd guess, and the saga side is a discard engine that ends on a two-creature Edict. 56.3% at ALSA 1.6 is a first-pick body that is good rather than broken — take it, don't overcommit to black for it.
Kain, Traitorous Dragoon: Low-priority rare despite the shell. The 2/4 body blocks well and jump gives it a real clock, but connecting hands your opponent a 2/4 — the cards and Treasures rarely outweigh that. 51.6% and a 30% play rate; drafters correctly leave it in the sideboard.
Malboro: Reasonable top-end with a real floor: swampcycling {2} means it's never a dead card, and the ETB is a discard plus four points of reach. 56.0% / +1.6 is honest six-drop value, so take it mid-pack as your one big black finisher rather than as a payoff.
Namazu Trader: Solid B common, exactly as LoL frames it: four toughness is the point. It brick-walls the 3/3s and survives the 3-damage removal that defines this format, and the Treasure smooths a splash. 54.5% with IWD only +0.8 means it holds the ground rather than winning the game — mid-pack pick.
Ninja's Blades: Strong Job Select rare. Three mana for a 2/2 body plus a repeatable loot-and-drain that snowballs is exactly the two-for-one shape WB and WR want, and it eats an opposing removal spell for the 1/1. 57.6% with IWD +5.0 — pick it early, and remember to kill opposing Job Select tokens.
Overkill: Premium removal — pick it as highly as Sephiroth's Intervention. Three mana at instant speed kills anything regardless of toughness, which matters because it answers the four-toughness creatures cheap burn can't. 58.7%, IWD +5.5, ALSA 2.2 and a 93.5% play rate: it's a first-pick common-slot effect in an uncommon.
Phantom Train: WB-only playable — LoL is right that it's premium there and unworkable elsewhere. The 4/4 trample body dodges sorcery-speed removal and grows off your own dying permanents, but 46.8% play rate and ALSA 6.0 reflect that most decks can't crew it or feed it. In WB take it over a middling creature; anywhere else, don't.
Poison the Waters: Sideboard card. The -1/-1 mode matters against the 1/1 hero tokens and go-wide starts, and the discard mode is a proactive answer to a bomb, but neither is worth a maindeck slot at 52.8% and 31% play rate. Board it in against WR/WG token draws.
Qutrub Forayer: Sideboard card. A 3/2 for three whose upside mode needs you to have already damaged something this turn; 12.6% play rate and 51.2% GIH confirm the format never found the combat trick. Graveyard hate mode is fringe against BG.
Reno and Rude: Filler despite the 72% play rate — 53.4% and IWD -0.3 mean drafters overplay it. A 2/1 menace connects early, but the format's boards clog fast and the impulse mode taxes you a creature or artifact for one card. Playable in aggressive BR, cuttable in BG grind.
Resentful Revelation: Take it early — this is the best non-removal common in the set. LoL's Golden Egg winner for a reason: two mana to fix your draw, stock the graveyard for BG, and turn dead late-game lands into a flashback card. 57.8% with +3.0 IWD across every archetype; there is no deck that cuts it.
Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER: Format-defining bomb — 62.1% GIH, IWD +9.6, seen at pick 1.3. A three-mana 3/3 that converts every dying creature into drain and every sacrifice into a card, and the flip end the game outright. Take it over anything; build black around it.
Sephiroth's Intervention: The format's benchmark common and genuine P1P1 material. LoL called it the #1 common overall after expecting four-mana removal to be too slow — 58.6% / +5.1 with 93.5% play rate settled it. Unconditional instant kill plus two life answers every four-toughness blocker; take it over most uncommons.
Shambling Cie'th: Filler. Entering tapped is a real cost in a midrange format, and the recursion demands a heavy noncreature count plus spare black mana every turn. IWD -2.3 says the value engine mostly does not fire; only a spell-dense UB or BR grind deck wants it.
Shinra Reinforcements: Late-pick overperformer for BG — 57.0% at ALSA 6.5 means you'll wheel it. A 2/3 for three blanks the format's ground attacks, the three life buys time, and the mill three actually feeds graveyard payoffs. Exactly the kind of card that quietly rounds out a curve.
Sidequest: Hunt the Mark: Premium removal despite the price — 59.9%/+6.1 beats every common kill spell in the set including Sephiroth's Intervention. Unconditional destroy with no restriction, plus a Treasure engine and a Yiazmat flip that the grindy games actually reach. ALSA 2.6 and 92% play rate; first-pickable in BG/WB.
Summon: Anima: Role-player, not a bomb. Six mana for a 4/4 menace that draws three over three turns and then edicts is real value, but OH 49.0% vs GD 54.9% shows it's a card you want to draw late, never in your opener. 52.6% overall — a mid-to-late BX playable, not an early pick.
Summon: Primal Odin: Bomb, and one of the best cards in the set — 62.3% with IWD +9.2. Chapter I is unconditional removal, so it two-for-ones before the 5/3 ever attacks, and chapter III refuels. Six mana in a removal-dense format is fine when the card generates value on arrival. Take it over almost anything.
Tonberry: Good aggressive one-drop, better in your opener than off the top. Enters tapped and stunned so it's a two-turn investment, but first strike deathtouch on your turn makes it an unblockable-ish attacker in a ground format. The 59.3% OH vs 52.0% GD split is the whole story: play it early or not at all.
Undercity Dire Rat: Reliable playable, low ceiling. A two-mana 2/2 that leaves Treasure behind is a fine early body that later fixes a splash or fuels artifact sacrifice. 55.3%/+1.1 puts it as a mid-tier common — starts in most black decks, and BR/BG sac builds take it a bit earlier.
Vayne's Treachery: Premium black common and a benchmark — 57.5% GIH, IWD +3.2, 91.7% play rate. Two mana kills most of the curve, and the kicker turns a spare token or Job Select hero into a hard answer for the four-toughness bodies blue keeps deploying. Take it early in any black deck.
Vincent Valentine: Strong rare, taken at 1.7 and earning it at 57.9% / +4.6. The counters accumulate for free in a removal-heavy format and the flip side is a trampling lifelinker that returns when it dies, so opponents cannot profitably trade with it. Best in BR/BG where you supply the removal.
Vincent's Limit Break: Sideboard card. It needs a creature already on board, doesn't beat bounce or exile, and the rebuy comes back tapped — a 22.9% play rate and 52.0% at ALSA 7.2 is the format telling you it's not worth a slot. Only consider it in a BR deck stacked with cheap attackers you want to trade up.
Zenos yae Galvus: Bomb rare. Five mana for a 4/4 plus a one-sided sweeper of the format's token clutter and 1/1 hero bodies is a blowout, and the flip is a win condition you rarely need. 59.2% with IWD +6.1 — pick it over any removal spell.
Zodiark, Umbral God: Buildaround rare, not a slam. Five black pips means mono-black-ish or a heavy BG/WB deck, and the ETB is symmetrical — it can whiff badly against a wide board. 54.1% with only 49.6% play rate is the honest read: powerful when castable, unplayable when not.
Barret Wallace: WR-only role-player. A four-mana 4/4 reach with no ETB is exactly the clogged-ground trap unless you actually have equipped creatures to fuel the attack trigger. 51.6% with 34% play — a body that gets outclassed the moment their removal shows up.
Blazing Bomb: Nice one-drop for UR specifically: the tiered spells and MV4+ payoffs the archetype is built on grow it, and it converts into a real removal spell later. 57.3% at ALSA 6.5 makes it a cheap wheel-able synergy piece — in a deck without four-mana noncreature spells it's a 1/1 that pings.
Call the Mountain Chocobo: Good R common, better than it looks. Four mana buys a 2/2 body, a land, and a flashback for the long games this format defaults into — that's three cards of value out of one slot. 57.4%/+2.6 at 75% play rate; a reliable mid-pack pick in any red deck.
Choco-Comet: The best red card below rare and the doctrine benchmark for it. Scalable removal that also leaves a 2/2 behind is a two-for-one at any X, and it kills the four-toughness creatures cheap red can't. 61.0%, IWD +6.9 — take it over almost every red rare; first-pickable in UR or BR.
Clive, Ifrit's Dominant: Overrated mythic — ALSA 1.8 but only 55.1% and IWD +2.9, below several commons. Six mana for a 5/5 whose ETB is a gamble on red devotion, and the flip costs another six. Playable in heavy mono-red-leaning UR or BR, but don't first-pick it over premium removal.
Coral Sword: Playable WR filler; Numot's "treat it as a combat trick" read is exactly right. Flash-attaching first strike for one mana wins a combat and leaves a permanent behind, but +1/+0 is negligible after that, and 54.5% / +0.4 at 40.6% play rate says it's the 22nd card in equipment aggro, not a pick you make early.
The Fire Crystal: Never play this. 40.8% GIH with a −9.3 IWD is one of the worst numbers in the set: four mana that affects nothing on board, in a format where the ground is already clogged and the tempo loss is fatal. It being a legendary Crystal rare is not a reason to take it.
Fire Magic: Underrated — take it far higher than its ALSA 4.1. A one-mana scalable sweeper that sweeps 1/1 hero tokens early and 3-toughness ground stalls late is exactly what this format wants; LoL flags Matt Nass P1P1'ing it at the Pro Tour. 57.5% with IWD +4.3 in the format's best pair, UR.
Firion, Wild Rose Warrior: Good but conditional — 56.5% overall with OH 58.5% above GD 55.1%, the signature of a card you want early alongside equipment. In a real WR Job Select deck the free copy-token is a huge tempo swing; in a deck with two Equipment it's a vanilla 3/3. Pick it if WR is open.
Freya Crescent: Narrow WR equipment role-player. Flying on your turn makes her the ideal carrier for a Job Select suit and the mana ability accelerates the next one, but a 1/1 does nothing outside that plan — the 58.0% opening-hand versus 52.6% drawn split is pure aggro-curve behavior. Wheels often; don't reach for it.
Gilgamesh, Master-at-Arms: Strong finisher, but conditional. A 6/6 for six is already fine top-end; the dig is a two-for-one only in WR or WU equipment decks — the 64% play rate is the tell that a third of the time you don't want it. 57.5% at pick 3.2 is honest.
Haste Magic: Cut it. 50.3% GIH with a 9.5% play rate and ALSA 8.1 means even red drafters pass it — a two-mana trick that grants haste is win-more in a midrange format where the ground is already jammed. Last-slot filler at absolute best.
Hill Gigas: Draft it as a Mountain. Six mana for a 5/4 trample haste is a real haymaker, but the format's cheap removal answers it for two, and OH 48.8% vs GD 52.7% shows it is dead weight early. The {2} mountaincycle is the reason it makes decks at all.
Item Shopkeep: Sideboard-to-filler. 53.0% with IWD -1.8 and a 26.8% play rate says the menace trigger is too conditional even in equipment decks. WR is much better than its reputation, but it wants Job Select pieces and playable bodies, not a 2/2 with a rider that needs one.
Laughing Mad: Filler. Discard-then-draw-two is card selection, not card advantage, and this format wins with bodies and removal rather than raw digging. 53.6% with IWD -0.1 and a 33% play rate is the honest read. Playable only in BR/UR builds with flashback and graveyard payoffs to discard into.
Light of Judgment: Marginal removal — five mana instant-speed for one creature is above the format's rate. 6 damage kills anything and the equipment rider punishes Job Select, but 53.7% with OH 50.2% marks it as a card you want drawn, not held. Playable if you're short on interaction; cut it when you hit 5-6 pieces.
Mysidian Elder: Filler. A 1/3 for three plus a 0/1 pinger only matters if you're casting a wall of noncreature spells, and even in UR the 52.3% and IWD -0.6 say it underdelivers. Playable 22nd card in a spells-heavy build, cut otherwise.
Nibelheim Aflame: First-pick bomb, one of the best cards in the set. 64.5% and IWD +10.9 at ALSA 1.9 — a one-sided sweeper aimed by your biggest creature that flashes back to also refill your hand. In a format that gums up on 3/3s this ends games outright. Take it over any removal spell and build red around it.
Opera Love Song: Below the bar. Both modes are marginal — two impulsed cards for two mana is slow, and a +2/+0 trick gets blown out in a format this removal-dense. 52.7% with negative IWD and 28% play rate makes it a 23rd card for an aggressive WR/BR build only.
Prompto Argentum: Good UR two-drop, not a splash. Haste 2/2 that curves out and then makes Treasure once your tiered spells hit MV4+; OH 57.0 above GD 56.0 confirms it is an early-game card you want in the opener. Solid mid-pack pick, weak outside UR.
Queen Brahne: Filler at 52.2% and IWD -0.5 despite a 4.5 ALSA — drafters take it earlier than it deserves. A 2/1 prowess must attack to make value, and 2/1s do not attack into this format's 3/3 walls. Only worth it in a UR-style spell-dense build, and even then it's a late playable.
Random Encounter: Unplayable. Six mana for a randomized, temporary board that returns to hand at end of turn is exactly what a removal-dense midrange format punishes, and a 3.2% play rate with 48.7% GIH is as close to unanimous as this data gets. Do not maindeck it even in RG.
Raubahn, Bull of Ala Mhigo: WR-only role-player, and a replaceable one. A 2/2 for two with a ward that costs your life total isn't a body you want in a stalled format, and the equipment-shuffle rider is win-more. 53.0% with IWD -1.3 despite a 3.5 ALSA — people take it too early.
Red Mage's Rapier: Weakest of the Job Select equipment; 50.7% with IWD −2.4 is a real negative. The 1/1 body only matters if you're casting spells the turn it attacks, and Equip {3} makes it slow to redeploy. Remember the doctrine in reverse — opponents kill the 1/1 and you've spent two mana for nothing.
Sabotender: Filler. A 2/1 reach body does not hold the ground in a format defaulted to 3/3s, and the landfall ping is chip damage, not a clock. 51.9% at 30% play — a last-few-slots card for a red deck short on two-drops.
Samurai's Katana: Premium uncommon and one of red's best cards below rare (60.0%, +4.6, ALSA 3.2). +2/+2 with trample and haste is immediate damage the turn it lands, and Job Select means it demands a removal spell just to slow it down. Take it over almost any red common in WR.
Sandworm: Weak uncommon, close to a trap. Five mana for a 5/4 haste sounds fine, but the land destruction is nearly blank — they just fetch a basic — and a big no-real-ETB body is exactly the shape that fails in a removal-dense format. 52.0% with IWD 0.0 and 35% play rate.
Seifer Almasy: Excellent rare, close to a bomb in a spells deck. 3/4 for four already blanks the cheap removal, and the double-strike-when-alone plus graveyard flashback recursion turns each connection into a free spell. 59.4%, IWD +6.1, ALSA 1.9 — first-pick in UR or BR where the instant/sorcery count is high.
Self-Destruct: Sideboard card. Turning your creature into a one-shot Lava Axe costs you the creature, and 50.6% with IWD -0.8 at an 18% play rate confirms drafters are right to leave it out. LoL only found it in the Unexpected Request steal-and-kill line — that's a two-card combo, not a maindeck plan.
Sidequest: Play Blitzball: Trap. 48.3% with IWD −4.2 and a 17.6% play rate — it does nothing the turn it lands, needs six combat damage in one swing to flip in a format that stalls on the ground, and then charges {3} to equip. Red aggro can't afford a three-mana blank. Leave it in the sideboard.
Sorceress's Schemes: Real card, but a late-game one. The 60.4 drawn vs 53.0 opening-hand split and ALSA 6.1 tell the story: it's dead early and a two-for-one engine once your yard has a removal spell to rebuy. LoL rated it near their format-best spell in BR; take it mid-pack in a spell-dense UR/BR deck, never over a body or removal.
Summon: Brynhildr: Trap-shaped rare — picked at ALSA 3.4, delivers 52.4% with IWD −0.2. A 2/1 for two whose impulse draw and haste-granting rarely convert on a clogged ground, and the Saga sacrifices itself. This is exactly the saga-creature-is-not-a-pillar case; take a removal common over it.
Summon: Esper Ramuh: Marginal at best: 52.8%, IWD 0.0, and OH 49.5% well under GD 54.9% — a late-game card, not a curve play. Chapter I only kills something if your graveyard is already full of spells, and the Wizard pump is near-blank. A 3/3 for four in red, so playable, but low priority.
Summon: G.F. Cerberus: A trap rare — early-picked at 2.9 ALSA and returning 52.4% with negative IWD. The copy chapters do nothing unless you already hold a real instant or sorcery on exactly those turns, and a 3/3 for four is standard fare on a clogged board. Fine as a UR body if you're spell-dense; never take it over Choco-Comet or Thunder Magic.
Summon: G.F. Ifrit: Filler. A 3/2 for three that loots twice then trickles mana is not a saga worth building toward — the doctrine holds, saga creatures aren't pillars outside Fenrir and Fat Chocobo. 51.0%, IWD -1.5, 41% play rate. Playable in a red deck short on threes.
Suplex: Excellent red common and an early pick — ALSA 3.6 at 89% play rate. Three damage at sorcery speed with exile matters against the set's recursion, and the artifact mode is live game one against Equipment and Vehicles. Just short of Thunder Magic; take it over most red creatures.
Thunder Magic: Premium removal, first-pickable common. Note the tiers are 2 / 4 / 8 damage, not what LoL's blurb says — the {3} Thundara mode killing a four-toughness creature at instant speed is what makes it the best red common. 58.4%, +3.7, ALSA 3.1; never pass it late in red.
Triple Triad: Trap. LoL's RB combo pitch is real but 51.5% / IWD -1.0 with a 27% play rate is the verdict: {3}{R}{R}{R} on turn six for a random top card in the format's worst-but-one pair (BR at 54.62%). Only worth it if you're already mono-red-ish and desperate for a haymaker.
Unexpected Request: Late-pick sideboard-to-23rd card, and LoL is right that nobody should take it early. Threaten effects need a board that's already ahead, which is why the opening-hand WR (49.7%) craters while drawn-later hits 55.4%. Only real in BR sacrifice or WR equipment shells — and BR is a bottom-tier pair.
Vaan, Street Thief: Trap — the doctrine's headline early-pick offender. A 2/2 for three needing a Scout/Pirate/Rogue tribe the set barely supports, taken at ALSA 4.3 for 46.5% GIH and IWD -4.4. It is actively losing games. Do not take it over a common removal spell; usually don't play it at all.
Warrior's Sword: Mid playable in WR equipment aggro. Job Select means four mana for a 4/3 body's worth of stats, but equip {5} makes it functionally a one-shot creature. 54.9% with IWD exactly 0.0 — it fills a curve slot, and remember the Job Select rule cuts both ways: opponents should kill the 1/1 while it's holding this.
Zell Dincht: Marginal rare, close to a trap. A 0/3 for three that only attacks well once you're at five-plus lands, and the mandatory end-step land bounce fights the extra-land upside every turn. 55.6% with the opening-hand WR above the drawn WR (56.8% vs 54.6%) says it's a turn-three play or a dead card. Fine 23rd in RG-lite; never early.
Airship Crash: Flexible role-player that's never dead. Cycling for two means the narrow half doesn't cost you a card, and the format's evasion premium means there's usually a flier or an Equipment worth killing. 53.2% with a 28% play rate reads as maindeck one, board the second.
Ancient Adamantoise: Genuine bomb, but a clunky one. 8/20 that soaks all damage aimed at you and your board simply ends ground combat, and dying cashes in ten Treasure. 58.0% with GD 61.0 vs OH 53.3 — dead weight in your opener, unbeatable on turn eight. Only in real green ramp.
Balamb T-Rexaur: Solid green common top-end at 56.0% with the flexibility that matters: forestcycling for {2} means it is never a dead draw when you're short on lands. A 6/6 trample with three life attached is a real finisher on a clogged ground, though six mana caps it as your last curve slot in UG/BG.
Bard's Bow: Fine green common, mid-pack pick. Three mana for a 3/3 reach body that answers the fliers breaking the stall is the actual sell; the equip 6 almost never gets paid. 55.2% with +0.7 puts it in the playable-not-exciting tier for UG/WG, and it's routinely there at pick 6.
Bartz and Boko: Good but not a bomb. Realistically a five-mana 4/3 that sometimes costs four and sometimes shoots a blocker — the Bird count green needs to make it a two-for-one usually isn't there. 56.2% with IWD +2.6 is a solid mid-pick, not a reason to commit to green.
Blitzball Shot: Marginal trick. +3/+3 and trample is the effect that actually punches through the format's 3/3 walls, but 53.4% and a 24% play rate say green decks don't want it — the removal density means your creature gets killed in response. Twenty-third card.
Cactuar: Unplayable outside a blink or sacrifice shell. A one-mana 3/3 trample that bounces itself every end step gives you one attack per replay, and re-casting it is your whole turn. 14% play rate is the verdict; the 51.2% comes from the few decks with a use for it.
Chocobo Kick: Green's best removal and a high pick in any green deck (57.5%, +3.1, 87.6% play rate). Two mana to bite is efficient, and the land-kicker mode is how green answers four-toughness bodies. GD 59.7% vs OH 54.3% just reflects that it needs a creature on board first.
Chocobo Racetrack: Overdrafted trap. Five mana that does nothing the turn it lands, then trickles 2/2s in a format where 3/3s already stare at each other — 51.5% with IWD -0.7 against ALSA 4.8 and a 60% play rate is the classic gap between how early it's taken and how it plays.
Clash of the Eikons: Conditional removal, playable but not a priority. One mana fight is efficient when it works, but you need a bigger body already on board, and the Saga modes are near-blank outside WG. 53.8% with IWD -0.1 says it's break-even — a fine 22nd card in a green deck with real creatures, not an early pick.
Coliseum Behemoth: Green's best uncommon top-end and the exception to the expensive-fatty trap: the ETB choice means it's never a blank, so seven mana buys a 7/7 trample plus a card or artifact/enchantment removal. 58.2%, IWD +4.1. Take it as the single seven-drop in a BG or UG deck, not as two of them.
Commune with Beavers: Filler. Card selection that doesn't affect the board is a losing trade in a removal-dense midrange format, and 21.8% play rate at ALSA 7.7 tells you green drafters correctly leave it in the pile. 53.9% is bin-quality. Only relevant if you're assembling Towns or a specific artifact/creature payoff.
Diamond Weapon: Fine top-end for BG, not an early pick. The cost reduction makes it a realistic six or seven drop in a graveyard deck, and preventing all combat damage to it means it simply cannot be blocked out — but it dies to any exile or -X/-X effect and does nothing the turn it lands. 50.5% opening-hand vs 57.1% drawn: play one, never two.
The Earth Crystal: Trap. 47.6% GIH with IWD −3.6 despite an ALSA of 4.0 — drafters keep taking it because it is a legendary Crystal rare, and it does nothing on arrival in a format with a clogged ground and dense removal. The counter-doubling needs a counters deck FIN does not support.
Esper Origins: Bomb rare — 63.6% / +8.0 with ALSA 2.0 and OH 62.7%, meaning it's excellent in your opener, not just late. Two mana surveil-plus-life is a cheap early smoother that later flashes back into a Saga producing cards, ramp, and a game-ending team pump. First-pick green, and it makes green worth being in.
Galuf's Final Act: Unplayable — the worst card in this batch. It's a combat trick that requires your creature to die to do anything, and the counters land after the trade you already lost. 45.7% GIH with IWD -5.4 at a 10.4% play rate is the format's clearest "never" signal. Leave it in the sideboard.
Gigantoad: Above-filler green common. Four toughness is the magic number here — it survives the format's cheap burn and holds the ground all game, and the seven-land clause occasionally matters in UG ramp. 53.2% with a 6.7 ALSA means you get these late; take them then.
Goobbue Gardener: Fine green common role-player: a two-mana blocker that survives most cheap removal and ramps you to four. Note the inverted split — OH 56.5 beats GD 54.1, so it's an early-game card that's dead late. Playable in every green deck, never an early pick.
Gran Pulse Ochu: Solid role-player, better than a one-drop looks. Deathtouch blanks the format's biggest ground creature all game, and the {8} pump gives late games a real mana sink once your graveyard fills. 55.4% at 67% play — a genuine BG piece and fine filler elsewhere.
Gysahl Greens: Filler. A two-mana 2/2 with a mostly irrelevant pump is exactly average (54.4%, IWD +0.3), and flashback {6}{G} is a real late-game mana sink that gives it a second body. Playable in a green deck short on two-drops, but never a card you're happy to first-pick.
Jumbo Cactuar: Trap — the doctrine's own example. Seven mana for a 1/7 that only connects if they have no blocker at all, in the most clogged-ground format available. 49.4% with IWD -1.8 while going around pick 4 (ALSA 4.1). Being rare is not a reason; leave it.
Loporrit Scout: Cut. A 3/2 for three that only pumps on your own creature drops is exactly the vanilla ground body this format has no room for, and 9.8% play rate at 49.4% means the field already agrees. Sideboard.
Prishe's Wanderings: Role-player, mostly for UG or a three-colour splash. Instant-speed fixing that finds Towns organically plus a +1/+1 counter is real, but 54.3% with IWD +1.4 means it's smoothing, not power. Mid-to-late pick, and it's the right way to acquire Towns rather than drafting them early.
Quina, Qu Gourmet: Cut it. A 2/3 for three whose token-doubling needs a token engine FIN's green doesn't reliably supply, and the sac outlet costs {2} per counter. 52.2% with IWD −1.4 is below-replacement even at 57.4% play rate. Green needs to be pushed on you anyway — this isn't the card that pushes.
Reach the Horizon: Filler ramp. Four mana for two tapped lands does not affect the board in a removal-heavy midrange format, and 53.3%/+1.3 is barely above replacement. It earns a slot in UG value-ramp or a three-colour build fixing a splash; anywhere else it's a cut.
A Realm Reborn: Unplayable in Limited. Six mana for zero board impact and a 0.6% play rate — no live WR data because nobody registered it, so the read is provisional, but a do-nothing enchantment in a removal-heavy midrange format is not close. Last pick.
Ride the Shoopuf: Solid role-player at 55.5% / +3.3 with OH above GD — you want it turn two, not turn eight. Free counters every land drop grow past the format's 3-damage removal ceiling, and the 7/7 mode gives late-game reach. Best in UG/BG where your creatures survive to stack counters.
Rydia's Return: Filler at five mana. The pump mode only wins games you're already winning on a wide board, and green rarely goes that wide here; the two-card regrowth is the mode you'll actually cast, which is why it's 55.7% drawn versus 48.7% in openers. A reasonable BG/WG 23rd card, nothing more.
Sazh Katzroy: The best card in this chunk and a first-pick bomb — 64.2% GIH, IWD +10.8, seen at 1.7. Four mana that replaces itself and then doubles counters every attack, which ends stalled boards in two swings. Green is the second-weakest colour; this is the reason to be in it anyway.
Sazh's Chocobo: Take it high. 60.0% with OH 66.4 is one of the most extreme opening-hand skews in the set — a one-drop that grows every land drop is a genuine threat on turn one and a blank on turn eight. Green's best cheap creature and a reason to open green; the doctrine's 'green needs pushing' applies, but this pushes.
Sidequest: Raise a Chocobo: Playable two-drop, ignore the flip. Four Birds is a condition you will rarely hit, so grade this as a 2/2 that occasionally grows on a land drop. IWD +0.3 says fine-not-good; it fills a WG or UG curve slot without demanding anything.
Summon: Fat Chocobo: One of only two saga creatures the doctrine treats as a genuine format card (57.7%, +3.8). A 4/4 that immediately makes a 2/2 is a two-for-one against a removal-heavy field, and the repeating trample turns a clogged board into damage. Top-two green common — take it over most green cards.
Summon: Fenrir: The best saga creature in the set by a wide margin, and a first-pick-quality uncommon: 61.1% with IWD +7.1 and a 63.9% opening-hand WR — it's better early, not a late synergy card. Three mana for a 3/2, ramp, a counter, and a card. Take it over most rares in green.
Summon: Titan: Bomb. A 7/7 reach trample for five is above rate on its own, and chapter III turns any other creature into a lethal trampler while the land recursion smooths mana. 60.1%, IWD +7.1, ALSA 1.9 — the reason to be green when green is open; first pick and it wins the games it's in.
Summoner's Grimoire: Underperforming rare — 51.0%, IWD +0.4, and only a 40% play rate. The Job Select body arrives for free, but cheating creatures in on attack needs a full grip and equip {3} to move it is slow in a removal-heavy format. Playable in a creature-dense WG deck, otherwise a late pick.
Tifa Lockhart: Skip the rare. 50.2% and IWD −1.4 make it one of the worst-performing rares in the set: a 1/2 trample for two that needs a land drop plus a pump-heavy board to matter, and doubling 1 power is nothing. Landfall is not a supported theme here. ALSA 3.8 means the table is still overpaying — let them.
Tifa's Limit Break: Marginal trick. The one-mana Somersault mode is the one you actually cast, and getting blown out by cheap removal in response is a live risk with 4-6 pieces per deck now standard. 53.2% and 39% play rate: playable in RG/WG aggro that has a trampler worth doubling, cut elsewhere.
Torgal, A Fine Hound: Strong green uncommon, better than it looks. Two-mana 2/2 that also taps for any color is real fixing and ramp, and the Human counter-buff is live in green's Human-dense builds. 58.6% with OH 61.5 above GD 56.4 — you want this on turn two, so take it early in UG/WG/BG.
Town Greeter: The #1 green common per LoL and the data agrees at 58.8% / +3.7 — take it well before its 5.1 ALSA. Two mana for a body plus a guaranteed land hit fixes a splash and mills four for BG graveyard payoffs. The 1/1 body is irrelevant; the card advantage and consistency are the point.
Traveling Chocobo: First-pickable green mythic, but green needs to be pushed on you before you commit. 58.9% with +5.7 IWD at a 1.8 ALSA is real card advantage — playing off the top means it out-grinds the removal war even after they kill it, and the trigger-doubling is a bonus. The 3/2 body dies to everything, so value it as an engine, not a threat.
Vanille, Cheerful l'Cie: Strong uncommon and a genuine BG payoff — a body that rebuys your best dead permanent is card advantage in the colour pair built on the graveyard. 58.5% with IWD +4.0 at a 3.5 ALSA. Ignore the Fang meld; you'll almost never assemble it.
Absolute Virtue: Bomb, and the protection clause ends games outright — they cannot burn you, block profitably, or race an 8/8 flier. IWD +7.9 is elite even for eight mana. WU is only mid-table at 55.7%, so take it as a finisher for any blue or white deck that can reach eight lands.
Balthier and Fran: Trap rare. A three-mana 4/3 reach is a real body, but every line of text needs Vehicles, and RG is the worst pair in the format at 53.4%. 52.6% with a 23% play rate — take it as a beater if you are already RG, never as a reason to be there.
Black Waltz No. 3: Underwhelming signpost. Flying deathtouch on a 2/2 is fine, but 51.4% with OH 48.4% says the spell trigger rarely fires enough to matter, and BR sits 9th at 54.62%. Play it if you're already BR; don't let it pull you into the pair.
Choco, Seeker of Paradise: Good body, punishing cost. A 3/5 blanks the format's ground creatures and the attack trigger is real card advantage, but {1}{G}{W}{U} means you're playing it only in an already-committed WUG or WG deck with fixing. 55.0% GIH with IWD +4.4 — it wins games when castable, so don't bend a two-colour deck toward it.
Cid, Timeless Artificer: Narrow build-around with a real floor. Cycling for {W}{U} means it's never dead, but the anthem only scales in a dedicated WU artifact/Hero deck with multiple Artificers. 55.5% at 52% play rate is the honest read: a good card in the 20% of WU decks built for it, a cycler otherwise.
Cloud of Darkness: Top BG signpost and a near-bomb uncommon — 60.0% with IWD +5.6. A 3/3 flier is already the evasion this format pays for, and the ETB scales into full removal by the mid-game since BG naturally stocks permanents in the yard. Note Numot's blurb mislabels it blue/black; it's BG, and the -X/-X wants graveyard density.
Emet-Selch, Unsundered: Premium UB mythic and the reason to be in the pair despite UB being 8th. Three mana for a 2/4 vigilance that loots on every attack is already a fine rate, and the flip is a game-ender in grindy games. 58.5% with IWD +8.1 and an identical OH/GD split means it's great at every stage. First-pickable.
The Emperor of Palamecia: High pick in the best pair. A proactive two-drop that ramps toward the Tiered payoffs is exactly what UR wants, and the 60.5% opening-hand (above its drawn rate) confirms it's a play-it-on-curve card, not a late-game top-deck. 59.1%/+4.8 for an uncommon; take it whenever you're U/R.
Exdeath, Void Warlock: Good BG signpost, worth a solid mid pick. Three-mana 3/3 with a life buffer that flips into a trampling threat once six permanents hit the yard — reachable in BG's graveyard plan, slow elsewhere. 57.8% with IWD +3.4 in the third-best pair; do not first-pick it out of color.
Garland, Knight of Cornelia: The best-performing card in the worst-but-one pair: 56.5% / +3.3, but BR sits ninth at 54.62%, so this is a signal-follower not a reason to force. A two-mana 3/2 that surveils on every spell is genuinely strong tempo, and the back-half flier gives late-game inevitability. Take it if BR is open.
Garnet, Princess of Alexandria: Playable two-drop, weak signpost. A two-mana lifelink legend is fine on its own, and WG at 55.88% is mid-table rather than the C-tier the experts called it — but the saga-counter payoff is a trap you rarely assemble, since saga creatures aren't format pillars. 55.7% with +1.0 and a 47% play rate says take it late in the pair.
Giott, King of the Dwarves: Synergy card, not a slam, despite the WR gold frame. Double strike on a 1/1 does nothing until you attach equipment, and the loot needs a Dwarf/Equipment stream. Classic high-GIH/flat-IWD shape: 56.3% but IWD -0.2 at 50% play. Only take it once WR is real.
Gladiolus Amicitia: The best card in the worst archetype. A 6/6 that fixes and turns every land drop into a trample pump is a legitimate 57.5% / +5.4 payoff, but RG is dead last at 53.4% — take it as a top-end body if you're already in one of the colours, not as a reason to enter the pair.
Golbez, Crystal Collector: Build-around trap. Four-plus artifacts by your end step is a demanding count, eight is fantasy, and the floor is a two-mana 1/4 wall. 49.9% GIH is the tell despite the +2.1 IWD; UB is already the 8th-best pair, so do not steer toward this.
Hope Estheim: Weak rare — 51.5% and a 31.9% play rate. Milling for lifegain does nothing in a format decided by board stalls and evasion, and WU (55.72%) wants fliers and equipment, not an incidental clock. A vanilla-ish 2/2 lifelink for two; last playable at best.
Ignis Scientia: Strong UG signpost and one of the best three-mana uncommons: 58.8%/+6.1 at 71% play rate. The land dig fixes a splash and hits your drops, and the graveyard-exile ability quietly hoses BG reanimation in a long game. UG is only 7th as a pair, so read the signals before committing.
Jenova, Ancient Calamity: Bomb-level BG signpost. A 1/5 body survives everything, the counters make a real threat every combat, and turning a doomed creature into a fistful of cards inverts removal against your opponent. 60.5% with IWD +8.2 and near-identical OH/GD — it's great in every slot. First pick in BG.
Joshua, Phoenix's Dominant: Excellent WR rare — first-pickable at ALSA 2.5, 58.0% with IWD +4.7. A three-mana 3/4 already beats the format's cheap removal on toughness and the loot smooths your hand; the flip side is pure upside you only pay for when the game goes long. Best gold card for the underrated WR aggro pair.
Judge Magister Gabranth: Good WB signpost, not a bomb. Menace on a two-drop that grows every time a permanent dies is a real clock in a format full of chump blocks and token trades, and 56.1% is solid — but IWD only +1.1 means it's a deck-quality card, not a game-winner. Take it as a WB commitment, not as a splash.
Kefka, Court Mage: First-pick bomb. 62.6% with a +12.8 IWD is the top of this chunk by a mile — a 4/5 that two-for-ones on every attack and flips into a flying draw engine. Three colours is the only cost, and UR or UB splashing the third pip is a completely normal landing spot.
Kuja, Genome Sorcerer: Bomb, and take it even though BR is the ninth-best pair. 62.1% GIH with IWD +10.2 and OH 62.5 — a 3/4 for four that walls the ground and builds an inevitability engine of pinging Wizard tokens every end step. It wins games on its own; the archetype tax is worth paying.
Lightning, Army of One: Strong mythic for the underrated WR pair (56.52%, and the experts had it too low). First strike plus lifelink on a three-mana 3/2 wins ground fights outright, and Stagger turns any follow-up burn into a real clock. 56.3% / +2.9 is good, not broken — it needs an aggressive shell.
Locke Cole: The best signpost in this batch — take it highly if you're in UB. Deathtouch plus lifelink is the perfect stat line for a clogged ground: nothing profitably blocks it, nothing profitably attacks into it, and every connection loots you toward your removal. +5.1 IWD is elite, and it carries a pair the data ranks only 8th.
Noctis, Prince of Lucis: Trap outside a built WUB artifact deck — a 22% play rate and 48.5% GIH say most drafters can't cast it. Three colours for a 4/3 lifelink whose recursion needs a graveyard full of artifacts. Leave it unless your artifact count is already double digits.
Omega, Heartless Evolution: Strong seven-drop because it's not a vanilla fatty — the stun counters buy two turns while an 8/8 closes. 57.9% / +5.4 is real, but OH 52.9 vs GD 60.9 flags it as a card you never want early. UG is a fine home; splash-friendly enough for any ramp deck.
Rinoa Heartilly: Strong WG uncommon and a real reason to be in the pair. Five mana buys two bodies plus an attack trigger that scales with your board — exactly the go-wide payoff WG wants. 57.1% with +3.4 IWD; a top-of-curve card, not a build-around.
Rufus Shinra: Solid WB playable. A three-mana 2/4 sits above the format's cheap removal and above most ground attackers, and it makes a 2/2 every time it attacks into an empty board. 56.7% with OH 58.6% means you want it early on curve; take it as a good uncommon, not a bomb.
Rydia, Summoner of Mist: Low-priority signpost — the card is fine, the pair isn't. Landfall rummaging smooths draws and saga recursion is real value, but a 1/2 body does nothing on a clogged board and RG is the format's worst deck by a full point. 53.7%/+1.0; take it as a marker, not a mandate.
Serah Farron: Trap outside a heavy legends deck. Two power for three with a cost reduction that needs legendary creatures you may not have, and a transform condition demanding two more. 51.0% with IWD -0.1 and 35.5% play rate — the field correctly leaves it out. WG legends only, and even then middling.
Shantotto, Tactician Magician: Premium UR uncommon — 59.0%, IWD +5.0, and near-identical opening-hand and drawn win rates, so it's good whenever it shows up. The 0/4 body sits above the format's cheap removal and blanks ground attackers by itself, then the tiered spells that make UR the best deck turn it into a threat that draws cards.
Sin, Spira's Punishment: Bomb if you can cast it. Seven mana across three colors is a real constraint, but a 7/7 flier that copies a permanent from your yard on ETB and every attack wins on the spot — 59.4% with IWD +8.6 and a 61.4% drawn WR. UBG value-ramp only; don't take it as a two-color splash without fixing.
Squall, SeeD Mercenary: Premium WB signpost. A 3/4 for four is already the right body for a format where four toughness dodges the common removal, and the recursion trigger means it grinds even after it's answered. 57.7%/+5.5 at ALSA 2.4 — first-pickable if you're open in white-black.
Tellah, Great Sage: Overdrafted rare — ALSA 3.0 for 54.4% GIH. Five mana for a 3/3 that only pays off if you untap and cast MV4+ noncreature spells, which is a UR-only ask, and by then a 3/3 body is easy to kill. Playable, but pick removal or a flier ahead of it.
Terra, Magical Adept: Skip unless RG is wide open — RG is the worst pair at 53.37%, and the 51.2% play rate shows drafters correctly leave it in the sideboard. The flip is a multi-turn project at six mana on top of three. As a 4/2 for three that mills five, it's fine; as a first pick, it's a color trap.
Tidus, Blitzball Star: Below replacement — the weakest signpost here. A 2/1 for three is dead on arrival against 3/3s and cheap removal, and the tap trigger only fires if it survives to attack; you need a genuinely artifact-dense WU build before the counters arrive fast enough. 51.3% with IWD -1.6 and a 46.9% play rate: skip it.
Ultimecia, Time Sorceress: Solid UB top-end — a 4/5 for five brick-walls the ground and the surveil smooths draws. Treat the flip as decoration; you'll rarely bank eight cards and ten mana. 55.0% with IWD +3.5 is fine, but UB is the 8th-best pair despite its reputation, so don't force it.
Vivi Ornitier: First-pick mythic and the signpost for the format's best deck. A three-mana engine that generates mana, grows, and drains every noncreature spell wins UR games on its own — 59.0% / +7.1 with 82.6% play rate. The 0/3 body dies to nothing cheap; protect it and the game ends fast.
The Wandering Minstrel: Fine two-drop, not a Towns engine. Five Towns almost never assembles and the five-color pump is decoration — what you get is a 1/3 blocker whose lands-enter-untapped clause quietly fixes a greedy mana base. OH 51.7% vs GD 58.2% shows it wants to arrive after the deck exists.
Yuna, Hope of Spira: Near-bomb and the strongest reason to be WG (60.4%, IWD +8.1). A 3/5 body already brickwalls the ground, ward {2} makes her hard to remove on your turn, and returning an enchantment creature every end step is unbeatable value in a grind. The 69.5% play rate is colour commitment, not weakness.
Zidane, Tantalus Thief: Strong WR uncommon and the pair is much better than its reputation (56.5%, second-best). The threaten-plus-lifelink ETB is a tempo swing and a life swing on an already-developed board, which is why drawn-later (60.1%) beats opening-hand (55.5%). 58.2%/+3.0 — a high pick if you're in red-white.
Adventurer's Airship: Filler. Crew 2 in a format where your two-power creatures want to attack is a real tax, and 18.3% play rate at 54.0%/IWD -0.8 says the field mostly leaves it in the sideboard. Resolving LoL's split: Ben is right, Ethan is wrong — a 3/2 flier that loots is not worth the crew cost.
Aettir and Priwen: The set's worst trap — 41.5% GIH and IWD -9.4, the largest negative in the format, yet it's still being taken around pick 4 at ALSA 4.4. Six to cast plus five to equip is eleven mana for a creature that dies to any removal spell in response. Never maindeck it.
Blitzball: Filler artifact, and remember the doctrine: it is NOT a five-color enabler. Three mana to ramp and eventually cash for two cards is fine in a legends-heavy WB deck, but 51.0% with IWD −0.7 says it mostly costs you a turn. 23rd card at best; never take it over a creature or removal.
Buster Sword: Pick it first. ALSA 1.2 with a 99% play rate and +6.9 IWD is as close to a mono-signal card as FIN has: +3/+2 turns any body into a clock, and equip 2 means it re-deploys after the removal spell. Numot's read holds — it's a reason to be in WR, the pair the experts under-rated.
Elixir: Unplayable. 46.0% GIH, IWD −2.6, 4.6% play rate — it enters tapped, costs six total to activate, and refills your library rather than affecting the board. Nothing in FIN mills you hard enough to want this. Last pick.
Excalibur II: Trap. 45.1% with IWD -5.7 is one of the worst numbers in the set, and only 15% of decks played it. A one-mana Equipment that starts at +0/+0 needs a lifegain engine you won't have, and equip {3} on top makes it slow even when it works. Do not maindeck it.
Genji Glove: A named trap — the doctrine flags it at 50.0% with IWD -2.2 despite a 4.1 ALSA. Five to cast plus three to equip is eight mana before it does anything, and the extra combat is worthless if the creature gets killed in response. Rare doesn't mean playable; pass it for any common removal spell.
Instant Ramen: Filler with an artifact tax. Two mana to draw a card at flash speed cycles, but you're spending a card slot on a cantrip unless you have real artifact or Food payoffs. 53.1% at an 18% play rate and 7.7 ALSA — last-pick territory, wheel it.
Iron Giant: Trap, and the numbers are brutal: 46.0% with a 6.4% play rate. Exactly the doctrine's expensive no-ETB creature — seven colorless mana for a body that does nothing on arrival in a format packed with four-mana kill spells. Never maindeck it.
Lion Heart: Overrated playable. The high play rate with IWD -0.4 is the doctrine's "good decks run this" shape — four mana for a Shock plus a +2/+1 aura is slow in a format where removal answers the carrier. Play it in WR equipment; do not take it over real removal.
Lunatic Pandora: Unplayable outside a desperate artifact-count deck — 49.5%, IWD -1.4, and only 13% of drafters who own it will run it. Surveil 1 for two mana is not a board presence, and a seven-mana total to destroy one permanent arrives long after the game is decided.
Magic Pot: Sideboard. A colorless 1/4 for three technically walls the ground, but it does nothing offensively and the graveyard-exile ability costs too much to matter. 48.9% with a 6.3% play rate is as close to unplayed as a common gets. Bring it in against BG reanimation only.
The Masamune: Hard trap and the doctrine's second-worst early-pick rare — 44.2% GIH, IWD -6.3, still taken around pick 4. Three mana plus equip 2 for first strike and a lure, with a death-trigger doubler that most decks have nothing to double. Legendary artifact is not a reason. Don't play it.
Monk's Fist: Filler. Two mana for a 2/1 Hero is a fine curve play in WR equipment, but +1/+0 is a rounding error and IWD -1.6 against 54.5% says it's a body that happens to be an artifact. Last-pick territory (ALSA 7.0) — take it only for artifact count.
PuPu UFO: Sneaky-good defensive uncommon. A two-mana 0/4 flier walls the format's 3-power ground and blocks the fliers that break stalls, and free land drops smooth out a greedy curve. 56.0% / +3.8 is real value; treat the Towns-pump as a bonus you'll rarely activate, not the reason to play it. Solid in WU/UG.
The Regalia: Near-auto-include. A colourless 4/4 haste that crews off a single 1/1 hero token, dodges sorcery-speed removal, and ramps you on every attack — that's why the play rate is 98%. 57.7%/+3.9 is strong without being a bomb; take it early, and it never gets stranded on colour.
Relentless X-ATM092: Colorless filler top-end for a deck short on finishers. Six mana for a 6/5 that is effectively unblockable on a clogged board is a real clock, but 51.7% with IWD −0.4 and 34.9% play rate say it costs too much in a format where the games are decided by cheaper interaction.
Ring of the Lucii: Filler at 53.6% and a 33% play rate. It ramps two and can tap a blocker or a would-be attacker each turn, which matters in a stalled format, but four mana that affects nothing on arrival is exactly the trap shape here. Playable in a slow WB/UB deck short on top-end mana.
World Map: Sideboard/fixing card, not a maindeck artifact. It costs you a card and a turn to do nothing to a board where the games are decided by creatures and removal — 51.8% at a 36.6% play rate. Only run it if you're actually splashing a bomb or a Town-heavy mana base needs the second mode.
Adventurer's Inn: Do not pick this early. The 55.0% GIH is survivorship: only 19% of decks run it, and those already have Town payoffs assembled. A colourless land that gains 2 costs you fixing in a two-colour deck. Take it pick 13+ once your Town count is real.
Balamb Garden, SeeD Academy: The one Town worth picking on rate — 58.2% / +4.0 with balanced OH and GD means it's a real land that costs you nothing, and the flip side is an evasive card-draw engine that breaks ground stalls. Ignore the 'don't take Towns early' rule for this one if you're UG or splashing.
Baron, Airship Kingdom: Late-pick land, never early. It fixes UR, the best pair in the format, and the 55.6% reflects the decks playing it rather than the card doing work. Per doctrine, Towns pay off when they accumulate organically — take spells first and let these wheel.
Capital City: Late-round land, not a pick. The 55.9% is what happens when a good deck plays a free fixer with cycling, not something the card causes. Doctrine is explicit: do not take Towns early. Wheel it, splash off it, and cycle it when your mana is fine.
Clive's Hideaway: Don't play it. Four-plus legendary creatures is not a Limited condition, so this is a colorless tapland with a dead ability. 47.4% GIH, 43.6% from the opening hand, 5.5% play rate — the worst kind of Town land. Rare doesn't matter; it isn't a card here.
Crossroads Village: Include it if your mana needs it, don't pick it early. An any-color tapland smooths a splash, and the 92% play rate reflects that it goes in most decks — but the +0.4 IWD is mana-fixing, not power. Never take it over a playable, and it is not a Town payoff worth chasing.
