Eden, Seat of the Sanctum: Late-pick Town, and the doctrine's rule holds: don't take Towns early. Colorless mana is a real cost, and the six-mana recursion is a slow one-shot. 55.4% with IWD +1.0 reflects the BG value decks that assemble Towns organically — it's the payoff, not the plan.
Gohn, Town of Ruin: Don't pick it early — a tapped BG dual is a fixing card, not a payoff. The 55.2% and +0.5 IWD are just "decks with good mana win more," not the land doing work. Take it late once BG is settled; Towns payoffs come together on their own, and a real spell always beats a tapland in the first half of a pack.
The Gold Saucer: Do not take Towns early. Colourless mana in a two-colour deck is a real cost, and the coin-flip Treasure and artifact-sac draw are win-more sinks. 53.3% at ALSA 7.5 means it wheels — pick it up last in a heavy artifact deck that wants the mana sink, otherwise leave it.
Gongaga, Reactor Town: Do not pick Town lands early. A tapped RG dual with 53.9% GIH and IWD +0.6 — the win rate is just "decks with good mana win," not card quality, and RG is the worst pair in the format. Take it late when Town payoffs have already accumulated organically.
Guadosalam, Farplane Gateway: Do not pick Town lands early — that's the doctrine, and the 6.1 ALSA reflects it. Its 55.4% is mostly the win rate of two-color UG decks that wanted the fixing, not the land's contribution. Take it late when UG is settled, or when a splash needs support.
Insomnia, Crown City: Don't pick Towns early — this is a last-pick land that costs you tempo entering tapped. It smooths a genuine WB deck and turns on Town payoffs if you've already collected several, but 53.5% with IWD -0.4 means it isn't improving your draws by itself. Take real cards over it every time until the last few picks.
Ishgard, the Holy See: Trap, and one the doctrine names by number — 52.4% with IWD -2.6 despite a 4.5 ALSA. It enters tapped, produces one colour, and the artifact/enchantment rebuy is a late-game luxury you pay for on turn three. Rare Town is not a reason to take it early.
Jidoor, Aristocratic Capital: Skip it. 49.3% with IWD −1.1 — a tapped land that later mills for no board impact does nothing in a midrange format where nobody dies to decking. Classic Town trap; take a playable instead unless you've somehow assembled a Town deck.
Lindblum, Industrial Regency: Modest rare being taken far too early at ALSA 4.2. The land half enters tapped for one color; the {2}{R} Wizard token is a small board add, not a threat. IWD -0.5 says it is roughly a free land slot for a mono-red-leaning deck, nothing more.
Midgar, City of Mako: The ALSA of 3.7 is the mistake here — 54.2% with IWD -0.3 says it plays like a tapped Swamp with a mediocre back half. Sacrificing a creature or artifact for two cards is a fine mana sink in BG, but a rare land is not worth a real pick over any of black's premium removal.
Rabanastre, Royal City: Playable WR fixing, never an early pick — the doctrine's rule on Towns holds. Entering tapped costs real tempo in a format where curve matters, and 53.8% with IWD -0.6 reflects that it smooths mana rather than winning games. Take it in the last few picks if you're red-white.
Sharlayan, Nation of Scholars: Playable land for WU only, and a late pick. Entering tapped is a real cost in a format where tempo decides stalls, and 54.3%/+0.8 is fixing value, not card quality. Take it if you're already committed to two colors that need it; otherwise it's the 40th card.
Starting Town: Take it for fixing, not for power. A 94.5% play rate and untapped-early-plus-any-color makes it the best Town in the set and the enabler for a splash. But 55.4% with IWD +2.0 is land-shaped value — pick it over filler, never over a playable, and only if you're actually splashing.
Treno, Dark City: Same read as the rest of the Town cycle: late-pick fixing for UB, not an early pick. +1.9 IWD is slightly above its cyclemates but still reflects mana quality rather than card quality, and the enters-tapped cost is real in a midrange format. Take it after your playables; a Towns payoff is a bonus, never a plan.
Vector, Imperial Capital: Late pick, fine in the right deck. A tapped dual is real fixing for BR or for a black-red splash, but entering tapped costs tempo in a format that punishes stumbles, and BR is a bottom-third pair anyway. 54.4% is the fixing tax showing up as a small positive; take it around pick 8+.
Windurst, Federation Center: Same read as every Town: late-pick only. Tapped GW dual, 54.0% GIH but IWD −0.1 — it costs you tempo and adds nothing to the board. Fine as a 17th land in WG or a splash enabler; never over a playable.
Zanarkand, Ancient Metropolis: Better than a Town land has any right to be at 56.2% and an 84% play rate, because it's genuinely free: a green source early, or six mana later for a Hero token the size of your land count. IWD is only +1.4 since it's a land, but the flexibility is real. Solid mid pick in green.
Adeline, Resplendent Cathar: First-pick bomb from the bonus sheet: 62.4% GIH with +7.5 IWD and a 65.3% opening-hand rate is the top non-Atraxa line in this batch. It makes a token every attack and grows with the board, which is exactly how you break a ground stall from the top down. Bonus-sheet samples are a few thousand games, so treat the exact number as noisy — the verdict isn't.
Ranger-Captain of Eos: Strong bonus-sheet pickup — 59.8% with IWD +3.8. Two mana for two bodies is real value in a format where 1/1 tokens are the default currency, and the sac ability protects a swing. Bonus-sheet samples are thousands of games, not hundreds of thousands, so treat the edge as directional.
Sram, Senior Edificer: Best bonus-sheet card in this batch. 59.9% / +4.1 with OH 62.7 says it's a two-drop that draws multiple cards in WR Equipment and WU artifact decks — Job Select equipment triggers it repeatedly. Small bonus-sheet sample, but the shape is unambiguous; take it if you're white.
Counterspell: Strong reactive card for UR/WU tempo. GD 60.1% vs OH 55.5% is the classic counterspell split — you want it drawn with mana up, not clogging an opener. Bonus-sheet sample is far smaller than the main set, so treat 58.4% as directional, but hard countering their best card is real in a grindy format.
Urza, Lord High Artificer: Best card in this batch and a first-pick-out-of-the-pack slam: 64.2% GIH with IWD +13.1 and a 91.2% play rate. The token, the mana engine, and the construct are three separate ways to break a stalled board. Bonus-sheet sample is small, but nothing at that IWD is a fluke.
Venser, Shaper Savant: One of the better bonus-sheet cards — flash, a body, and a bounce that answers anything including a spell, which is exactly the tempo blue wants. 57.8%/+3.7 at ALSA 2.9 and 87% play rate. Caveat: bonus-sheet samples are thousands of games, not hundreds of thousands, so treat the number as softer than a real common's.
Bolas's Citadel: Bonus-sheet rare with a small sample — treat the numbers loosely. Six mana that does nothing to the board is a rough ask here, but the top-of-library engine wins the game outright when it lives. GD 59.2% vs OH 52.9% is the tell: fine as a late-game draw, a liability in your opener.
Dark Ritual: Skip it. Ritualing out a four-drop on turn two is card disadvantage in a midrange format where the ground gums up and the opponent has four-plus removal spells. 51.8% on a bonus-sheet sample of a few thousand games — small sample, but the read matches the card.
Fatal Push: One of only two bonus-sheet cards that actually landed. 58.8% and IWD +4.9 put it right at the Sephiroth's Intervention tier — instant-speed one-mana removal that answers most of the format's early curve, though the MV-2 cap misses the four-toughness bodies that define the ground. Small sample; still a top black pick.
Syr Konrad, the Grim: Bonus-sheet card on a much smaller sample, so treat the numbers loosely. ALSA 2.9 and an 87.9% play rate say drafters take him early, but 54.6%/+2.0 says he's a good five-drop rather than a bomb — he needs a BG deck with creatures dying and cards leaving the yard to actually close games.
Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: Bonus-sheet bomb — take it. 62.6% GIH, IWD +9.8, ALSA 2.0. A repeatable sacrifice-to-shrink engine is oppressive against a board of 1/1 hero tokens and 3/3s, and it draws you cards doing it. Caveat: bonus-sheet samples run a few thousand games, so the number is noisier than a set common's.
Ancient Copper Dragon: Bonus-sheet mythic to fade — 51.8% with IWD -1.4 on a small sample, and LoL calls it fun RNG. Drafters take it at 2.5 on the name; the treasures only arrive if it connects, and this format's boards do not let a fatty attack for free. Play it as red top-end, don't first-pick it.
Godo, Bandit Warlord: Good WR equipment payoff, take it if you have the artifacts. The tutor-plus-extra-combat plan lines up with the equipment/Job Select deck the data ranks second at 56.52%, and 55.5% with +1.6 backs it. Bonus-sheet sample is small, and a 58.4% play rate says plenty of drafters correctly leave it out of non-equipment decks.
Purphoros, God of the Forge: Trap — the classic bonus-sheet reprint that misses. 49.6% GIH with IWD -3.4 and a brutal 43.9% opening-hand rate, yet drafters take it at pick 3.0. Red devotion rarely turns it on, so you're paying five for an enchantment that pings. Small sample, but the direction is clear.
Azusa, Lost but Seeking: Provisional — no WR data and a 22% play rate says most drafters cut it. Extra land drops do very little in a 17-land Limited deck with no landfall payoffs beyond a couple of cards; unless you have Sazh's Chocobo or Gladiolus, it's a 1/2 that does nothing. Low pick.
Nyxbloom Ancient: Provisional read — no win-rate data and only 20% play. Seven mana for a big trample body with a mana-tripling ability you rarely get to use is the expensive-fatty trap; the ramp only matters if you already have an expensive sink. Play it as a finisher in a slow green deck, nothing more.
Jodah, the Unifier: The +11.5 IWD is a selection illusion — only 28.3% of drafters who see it can cast {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}, and those are already the greediest fixed decks. Treat it as unplayable unless you have four-plus Towns and real fixing; then it's a haymaker.
Tymna the Weaver: Good in WB, which is a solid fourth-best pair. Lifelink on a cheap body matters in a grindy format, and the draw trigger converts a stalled board into cards — 57.3%/+3.9, with the opening-hand WR (59.0%) above drawn, so it's an early-game card. Bonus-sheet sample is small; take it as good, not a bomb.
Winota, Joiner of Forces: The best card in this chunk by a mile and a genuine bomb — 64.4% GIH, IWD +10.4, identical opening-hand and drawn numbers, so it wins from anywhere. WR is the second-best archetype and full of Hero tokens and non-Humans to trigger it. Small bonus-sheet sample, but nothing at +10.4 is noise.
Traxos, Scourge of Kroog: Playable colorless beater for artifact decks. A four-mana 7/7 that enters tapped and only untaps off historic spells needs equipment or legends to stay online — WR and WB can do it. 54.6% with IWD +1.9 is mid, and the bonus-sheet sample is thin, so treat it as a good body with a real drawback, not a bomb.
Akroma's Will: Bomb-tier bonus-sheet card at 63.6% and IWD +10.1 — effectively a one-card win condition once the ground stalls, which is FIN's default board state. Granting the whole team flying breaks the exact stall this format produces. Bonus-sheet samples are thin, but nothing about the card argues against the number. Take it.
Danitha Capashen, Paragon: Good in equipment decks, unremarkable elsewhere. 55.8% GIH against just +0.7 IWD is the 'good decks run this' shape again — a three-mana 2/2 body needs the first strike plus lifelink to matter, and the equip discount only pays in WR. Small bonus-sheet sample; take her as a solid mid-pick, not a reason to move in.
Kenrith, the Returned King: One of the two bonus-sheet cards worth a high pick. 58.7% with IWD +6.4 at ALSA 1.9 — a five-mana body with four mana sinks means it never draws dead, and the haste/trample modes break the ground stall. Smaller bonus-sheet sample, so treat the number as directionally right, not exact.
Loran of the Third Path: Strong bonus-sheet rare at 59.8% / +3.7, though the small bonus-sheet sample means less confidence than the number implies. A body plus artifact/enchantment interaction is exactly what white wants against Job Select equipment and White Auracite. Early pick in WR/WU; provisional read on the exact rate.
Mangara, the Diplomat: Overdrafted defensive rare — 53.3% and IWD +0.3 despite a 2.4 ALSA. Four toughness makes it a real blocker in this format, but the card draw is entirely conditional on opponents choosing to trigger it, and good opponents simply don't. A playable white body; never take it over a removal spell.
Stroke of Midnight: Underperformer, not the clean answer it looks like. Handing back a 1/1 in a format where the ground already gums up with hero tokens is a real cost, and three mana sorcery-speed-ish interaction is slow. 49.2% with IWD -2.6 — play it only if you're short on removal.
Wall of Omens: Solid white playable and a perfect fit for the format read — a four-toughness blocker that replaces itself blanks the aggro starts and survives the cheap removal. 57.6% / +3.3 confirms it. Small bonus-sheet sample, but this card has been good in every format it has touched; a fine mid-pick.
Brainstorm: Cut it. Without fetch lands or shuffle effects it is card selection that stacks two dead cards back on top, and Limited decks cannot afford the tempo. 53.6% with +0.8 IWD and a 44% play rate is a card riding good UR decks, not helping them.
Cryptic Command: Premium and worth building toward: 62.6% with GD 65.1% is elite, and the two-for-one modes are exactly what UR and UB grind decks want. The {1}{U}{U}{U} is a genuine cost in a two-colour format, so take it in blue and don't skimp on Islands. Bonus-sheet sample is small.
Laboratory Maniac: Unplayable. There is no self-mill route to actually decking yourself in a 40-card game, so this is a vanilla 2/2 for three. 49.3% with IWD -2.2, a 42.0% opening-hand WR, and a 6.2% play rate — the rare card almost nobody registers, correctly.
Rhystic Study: Trap in Limited, despite the mythic line. 47.8% GIH is the worst number in this chunk — a three-mana do-nothing enchantment that your opponent just pays for while you fall behind on board. Small bonus-sheet sample and the positive IWD is deck-quality noise. Don't play it.
Teferi, Mage of Zhalfir: Marginal. The 3/4 body survives the format's cheap removal and locking opponents to sorcery speed is genuinely annoying, but 51.7% with IWD +0.0 and a 43.6% play rate means it isn't converting. Bonus-sheet small sample, so the read is soft — playable in WU tempo, not a pick you prioritize.
Deadly Dispute: Solid role-player, not premium. 56.4% with IWD only +2.2 is the shape of a card good decks run rather than one that wins games alone — it needs a token or artifact to eat, so it's a BG/WB card. Fine mid-pick if you have Job Select equipment or Hero tokens; skip if your board is all real creatures.
Diabolic Intent: Trap. Sacrificing a creature to tutor is straight card disadvantage in a removal-dense midrange format where bodies are the resource — 48.1% with a −2.3 IWD and a 28.8% play rate confirms it. Bonus-sheet sample is small, but this is not a rare worth a slot; pass it.
Gix, Yawgmoth Praetor: Strong bonus-sheet mythic, first-pickable in black. 59.4% GIH, IWD +6.0, OH 60.4 — a four-mana body that converts the format's constant combat damage into cards is exactly the grind engine BG and WB want. Bonus-sheet sample is small; the read is solid but less settled than a common's.
K'rrik, Son of Yawgmoth: Trap — 44.6% with IWD -5.3 is a card that actively loses you games, and only 31% of drafters who opened it played it. Paying life instead of black mana does nothing in a Limited deck without a critical mass of black spells, and the body dies to everything. Sideboard.
Varragoth, Bloodsky Sire: Trap shape — picked around pick 3 at 2.6 ALSA and returning 53.0% with negative IWD. Boast is slow, tutoring costs you a turn of pressure with a fragile 3/2, and Limited decks rarely have the single card worth the detour. The bonus-sheet sample is small, but the read matches the doctrine's early-rare warning: pass it for interaction.
Captain Lannery Storm: Good red aggro card and one of the bonus sheet's few hits — 57.8%, IWD +3.2, 82% play rate. Haste plus Treasure means it converts into a real tempo turn even when it trades. Red is the weakest colour, so this is a fine mid-pick, not a reason to be there.
Light Up the Stage: Marginal. 55.0% with IWD +0.2 and a 48.7% play rate — the spectacle discount rarely comes online in a midrange format where you aren't reliably connecting, and the two exiled cards expire fast. Playable filler in an aggressive WR or UR deck, not a card to prioritize.
Lightning Bolt: First-pickable removal and one of only two bonus-sheet reprints that actually landed. One mana for three damage kills most of the format at instant speed and goes to the face when the game is over. 59.9% with +5.8 IWD and ALSA 2.5; smaller sample than main-set cards, but the effect needs no defense.
Mizzix's Mastery: Marginal. 53.1% with OH 48.5% means it's dead early and only mediocre later — Limited decks rarely have a target worth the sorcery, and red is already the weakest colour at 55.68%. Sideboard unless your UR deck is stuffed with expensive tiered payoffs to rebuy.
Najeela, the Blade-Blossom: Disappointing for a mythic — 53.9% with IWD +1.3 while being taken around pick 3.6. The token engine needs a wide Warrior board and free mana this format doesn't hand you, so it usually reads as a fragile three-drop. Playable if you're red, but it isn't the pick that wins the pack. Small bonus-sheet sample.
Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer: Strong but front-loaded — take it early in red aggro, discount it later. OH 62.5% vs GD 55.6% is the sharpest split in the set: a one-drop that only pays when cast on turn one. Small bonus-sheet sample. Great in WR or BR curve-out decks, mediocre topdeck in a grindy UR pile.
Carpet of Flowers: Unplayable — a 1.6% play rate and no win-rate sample at all. It does literally nothing unless your opponent is in blue, and even then it's a do-nothing enchantment in a format that punishes blank turns. Sideboard at best; the read is provisional only because no one played it.
Farseek: Leave it. 52.9% and IWD −0.7 confirm that a two-mana ramp spell that doesn't fetch basics is close to dead weight in a two-color midrange format — you're spending a turn to not affect the board. Only relevant if you're actually splashing off Towns in UG, and even then the Town lands do the job.
Fynn, the Fangbearer: Solid green two-drop. Deathtouch on a cheap body trades up all game long, which is exactly what you want when 3/3s and 4-toughness blockers are staring at each other — the poison text is mostly decoration in Limited. 55.7%/+1.9 on a small bonus-sheet sample: a fine early-mid pick, not a build-around.
Nature's Claim: Sideboard only. 51.5% GIH with IWD −0.8 and a 15% play rate — the cheap artifact/enchantment answer is live against Job Select equipment and the Crystals, but too narrow to main-deck. Bring it in post-board against WR equipment decks.
Primeval Titan: Bomb on the bonus sheet: 60.8% / +8.3 with ALSA 1.9 — a 6/6 trample that fetches two lands (Towns included) breaks a stalled board and refills your mana. Small bonus-sheet sample, so treat the exact rate as soft, but the card is real. First-pickable if you're green or splashing.
Atraxa, Grand Unifier: The biggest bomb you will see: 66.4% GIH with IWD +19.6 is not noise even on a small bonus-sheet sample. Seven mana across four colors means you're either ramping to it or reanimating it, so it's a payoff for UG value-ramp or BG reanimation rather than a card you cast on curve. Take it, then build toward it.
Bruse Tarl, Boorish Herder: Near-bomb in WR, the format's underrated aggro pair — 61.9% with IWD +7.1. Double strike plus lifelink on your biggest attacker is 6-8 damage out of nowhere against a stalled board. Bonus-sheet sample is small, but the margin is far too wide to be noise.
Dovin's Veto: Sideboard at best; 48.3% with IWD −1.4 and a 9% play rate. Uncounterable is irrelevant in Limited, WW-U-ish costing is awkward in a two-colour deck, and it can't touch creatures in the most creature-dense colours. Syncopate is the blue counterspell you actually want.
Inalla, Archmage Ritualist: Provisional — no win-rate data, 14% play. A three-color UBR gold rare is a mana-base problem before it is a payoff, and neither UB (8th) nor BR (9th) is a pair you want to be stretching from. Only playable if you are already deep in the wedge with fixing.
Ishai, Ojutai Dragonspeaker: Cut it. 45.5% with IWD -2.8 is one of the worst numbers in the set, and 30% play rate says most drafters correctly leave it in the sideboard. Its counters depend on opponents casting spells on your turn, which is not how a midrange ground format plays out.
Isshin, Two Heavens as One: Provisional read, no live WR and only an 8.3% play rate — it's simply not castable in a two-colour deck. {W}{B}{R} for a 3/3 whose text does nothing unless you're already attacking with trigger creatures. Treat it as a non-card unless you're base WB with heavy red fixing.
Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy: Marginal. A three-mana legend whose ramp only matters if you have mana abilities to untap and whose activated ability is a big-creature engine this format doesn't reward. 55.5% at 46.7% play rate on a small bonus-sheet sample — a fine body in UG, not a reason to be there.
Kraum, Ludevic's Opus: Good UR playable — 56.9% with IWD +4.1. A four-mana 3/3 with flying and haste is exactly the evasive clock that breaks a stalled board, and the draw trigger fires often in a deck full of cheap tiered spells and removal. Bonus-sheet sample is small, so hold the number loosely, but the card matches the archetype.
Muldrotha, the Gravetide: Take it and build to it. 58.6% with IWD +9.5 is bomb territory — a six-mana body that replays a permanent every turn simply cannot be beaten by the removal-trade grind FIN defaults to. UBG only, so make sure your fixing is real; the 60.5% drawn WR vs 55.5% opening-hand says it's a mid-game payoff.
Thrasios, Triton Hero: Role-player with a late-game sink. The 1/1 body is irrelevant, but a repeatable four-mana card-selection ability gives a UG value-ramp deck something to do with flooded turns. 55.0%/+1.7 and only 64.9% play rate on a small bonus-sheet sample — a fine mid-pick in UG, a blank in an aggressive deck.
Vial Smasher the Fierce: Playable bonus-sheet mythic, not a slam. IWD +4.8 looks strong but 55.8% GIH and a 77.4% play rate say it is a good body whose damage trigger needs a spell-dense BR deck to matter — and BR is ninth of ten. Take it in black-red, pass it otherwise; small bonus-sheet sample.
Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow: Skip. 51.6% with OH 47.7% badly under GD 53.9% means it's a card you can't afford to keep in an opener, and UB is only eighth at 54.90%. A 1/2 commander-format engine needs unblockable enablers this format doesn't reliably provide. Fringe playable, never an early pick.
Chromatic Lantern: Trap — 48.4% with IWD -0.9 and only a 47% play rate. It's a three-mana artifact that affects no board in a removal-dense midrange format, and FIN's Towns already give you the fixing a splash needs. Take almost any playable creature or removal spell over it; run it only for a genuine multi-color bomb.
Smuggler's Copter: First-pick artifact, colourless, goes in every deck — 64.2% GIH, IWD +9.2, ALSA 1.6, 99% play rate. A 3/3 flier for two that loots is exactly what a removal-heavy ground stall can't beat, and any 1/1 hero token crews it. Take it over almost anything.
Strixhaven Stadium: Do not play it. 45.6% and a 2.5% play rate — a four-mana artifact that does nothing to the board and needs many combat damage triggers to pay off is exactly wrong in a removal-heavy, gummed-up format. Tiny bonus-sheet sample, but the verdict is not close.
Command Beacon: Sideboard. A colorless land whose only ability returns your commander to hand does nothing in a Limited deck, and the 0.3% play rate confirms it. Do not slot it over a basic — the colorless mana costs you more than the land gains.
